headline: Anthropic has added a rule to its usage policy that bans users from sustained, needless cruelty toward its Claude AI models, and says it will apply only in extreme cases.
score_reason: Viral floor 9: about 30 outlets, BBC and CBS News lead
importance_line: From 12 Nov 2026 Claude users will have a conduct rule on how they treat the AI itself, but Anthropic says it targets only extreme, repeated cruelty and has not said exactly what counts as abuse.
summary: CBS News reports that Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, has added to its usage policy a ban on "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its AI models, which Anthropic announced on 8 Oct 2026 and says applies only in "extreme cases where users repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose", not to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research". Anthropic says the updated policy, which lists the clause beside bans on bullying and non-consensual intimate imagery, takes effect on 12 Nov 2026, and that Claude's existing ability to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users, on Claude.ai and in its coding tool Claude Code, stays the main way to enforce it, while CBS says the company did not immediately say what counts as abusive or how a conversation would be ended. The change, first reported by The Verge and part of a yearly update that also adds rules on deceptive campaigns, narrows the election rules and clarifies the weapons rules, was carried by about 30 news outlets and drew praise and criticism amid a wider debate about AI consciousness: the BBC reports criticism from Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at the Irish law firm William Fry, and CBS recalls that Mustafa Suleyman, chief executive of Microsoft AI, argued last month that Anthropic is effectively "training Claude that it may be conscious". Gizmodo reports that Elon Musk, chief executive of the rocket and AI company SpaceXAI, replied "I think this is the right move" to a post by Aaron Levie, chief executive of the software company Box, who had called the rule an "easy Pascal's wager"; we carried the policy as a short item in our 9 Oct 2026 edition.
